data.title: What OR Royalties (TSX:OR)'s Japan Gold Royalty Buy Means For Shareholders
data.description:
• OR Royalties has paid US$3 million to acquire an additional 0.5% net smelter return royalty over all Japan Gold Corp properties, increasing its total royalty interest to 2.0%.
  • The expanded royalty position gives OR Royalties broader exposure to Japan Gold's exploration portfolio while Japan Gold directs the cash into drilling capacity, non alliance projects, and working capital.
  • The next area of attention is how OR Royalties' larger royalty stake in Japan Gold shapes the broader investment narrative for the business.

OR Royalties Investment Narrative Recap

To own OR Royalties, you need to believe that its royalty and streaming portfolio will keep converting partner mine activity into high margin cash flow, even with heavy exposure to precious metals pricing. The Japan Gold royalty top up supports that idea only at the margin, because it is a small check against a roughly US$1b liquidity pool and does not shift the near term story.

The bigger short term swing factor still sits with execution at key growth assets like Canadian Malartic and the ramp up projects that are expected to add gold equivalent ounces. The main risk remains external. A pullback in gold and silver prices or delays at partner mines could hit royalty volumes or unit economics faster than incremental deals like Japan Gold can offset.

The Japan Gold transaction lines up most cleanly with management’s long running message that OR Royalties wants accretive royalties and streams while keeping capital discipline. A US$3 million royalty purchase is small against the balance sheet, yet it adds another jurisdiction and early stage pipeline exposure as Japan Gold allocates the proceeds to exploration and drilling capacity.

For you as a shareholder, the operational question is whether a steady cadence of these compact royalties, added to larger levers such as potential Canadian Malartic Odyssey shaft expansion or projects such as Dalgaranga and Namdini, actually translates into the revenue growth analysts currently model. Execution risk at partner projects and the firm’s ability to source deals that clear its cost of capital remain the real catalysts to track.

OR Royalties' current analyst narrative points to revenues of $561.3 million and earnings of $386.8 million by 2029, based on revenue growth of 15.7% per year and an earnings increase of about 37% from $283.1 million today.

data.title: What VAT Group Doubters Got Wrong
data.description:
If VAT Group was on your watchlist instead of in your portfolio over the last year, the result may feel like a miss. Investors who held VAT Group over the past year are up 59.4%, including dividends. That move arrived while analysts argued over whether digitalization and onshoring would reshape semiconductor manufacturing enough to justify bullish assumptions. The real question now is how you could have judged that manufacturing shift before the share price reflected it.

VAT Group has already moved. Pinpoint other ways to investigate the theme among 89 robotics and automation stocks.

The Two VAT Group Stories Investors Had To Balance

The shares cost CHF333 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at VAT Group then had to choose between two very different futures that both sounded plausible.

On the optimistic side, the bullish narrative argued that digitalization and onshoring would redraw semiconductor manufacturing. It pointed to a Fair Value of CHF410, essentially the price implied if those growth assumptions played out. That view leaned on analyst expectations for faster specification win conversions as new fabs ramped up.

The bearish narrative pointed to cyclical exposure and geopolitics, with a Fair Value of CHF260 based on more constrained outcomes. This camp focused on risks from semiconductor concentration and the possibility that export controls and supply chain disruption would cap VAT Group’s earnings power.

What The Evidence Around VAT Group Actually Tested

VAT Group’s later update that Q3 2026 brought the highest quarterly order intake and sales on record, with orders roughly tripling year on year, clearly leaned toward the optimistic digitalization and onshoring case. The H1 2026 report pulled the other way. Revenue and net income both fell compared with H1 2025, even though net margin edged up to 19.3%. Taken together, the evidence cut both ways.

The hinge assumption here was not abstract “growth” but how fast semiconductor demand would show up in booked orders and then in revenue and profit. When you test a similar story elsewhere, track order intake trends, conversion into sales, and whether margin direction matches the original promise.

What VAT Group's Current Price Already Assumes

VAT Group now trades at CHF517 after a 59.4% gain over the past year. The selected Narrative’s Fair Value sits below the current price, suggesting that today’s level already reflects strong wafer fab equipment demand and smooth execution of the expansion plan.

For that to be the case, capacity additions and the growing installed base would need to translate into resilient service income and margins despite ramp costs and currency pressure.

"The main requirement is that VAT Group successfully converts its expanded capacity, higher order book, and growing installed base into sustained service and product revenues that support margins despite currency and ramp-up cost pressures."

Looking Beyond VAT Group

VAT Group puts you close to the semiconductor buildout. You can still ask what sits just next to that story.

Those chips and tools only matter if the digital infrastructure around them keeps running. That requires reliable power and cooling for data-heavy businesses.

Another specialist focuses on the hardware and services that keep data centres powered, cooled, and monitored. Its systems help AI, e-commerce, and online banking stay available.

This is where physics, not hype, calls the shots. As computing loads intensify, the role of that quiet infrastructure provider could quietly expand.

data.description:
Last week saw the newest quarterly earnings release from S.J.S. Enterprises Limited (NSE:SJS), an important milestone in the company's journey to build a stronger business. S.J.S. Enterprises missed revenue estimates by 2.9%, coming in at₹2.8b, although statutory earnings per share (EPS) of ₹17.91 beat expectations, coming in 2.9% ahead of analyst estimates. Earnings are an important time for investors, as they can track a company's performance, look at what the analysts are forecasting for next year, and see if there's been a change in sentiment towards the company. So we collected the latest post-earnings statutory consensus estimates to see what could be in store for next year.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Following the latest results, S.J.S. Enterprises' five analysts are now forecasting revenues of ₹11.3b in 2027. This would be a satisfactory 7.2% improvement in revenue compared to the last 12 months. Statutory per share are forecast to be ₹70.05, approximately in line with the last 12 months. Before this earnings report, the analysts had been forecasting revenues of ₹11.3b and earnings per share (EPS) of ₹70.05 in 2027. So it's pretty clear that, although the analysts have updated their estimates, there's been no major change in expectations for the business following the latest results.

Check out our latest analysis for S.J.S. Enterprises

The analysts reconfirmed their price target of ₹2,768, showing that the business is executing well and in line with expectations. Fixating on a single price target can be unwise though, since the consensus target is effectively the average of analyst price targets. As a result, some investors like to look at the range of estimates to see if there are any diverging opinions on the company's valuation. The most optimistic S.J.S. Enterprises analyst has a price target of ₹2,950 per share, while the most pessimistic values it at ₹2,650. This is a very narrow spread of estimates, implying either that S.J.S. Enterprises is an easy company to value, or - more likely - the analysts are relying heavily on some key assumptions.

Another way we can view these estimates is in the context of the bigger picture, such as how the forecasts stack up against past performance, and whether forecasts are more or less bullish relative to other companies in the industry. It's pretty clear that there is an expectation that S.J.S. Enterprises' revenue growth will slow down substantially, with revenues to the end of 2027 expected to display 15% growth on an annualised basis. This is compared to a historical growth rate of 22% over the past three years. Compare this to the 143 other companies in this industry with analyst coverage, which are forecast to grow their revenue at 12% per year. Factoring in the forecast slowdown in growth, it looks like S.J.S. Enterprises is forecast to grow at about the same rate as the wider industry.

The Bottom Line

The most obvious conclusion is that there's been no major change in the business' prospects in recent times, with the analysts holding their earnings forecasts steady, in line with previous estimates. Happily, there were no real changes to revenue forecasts, with the business still expected to grow in line with the overall industry. There was no real change to the consensus price target, suggesting that the intrinsic value of the business has not undergone any major changes with the latest estimates.

data.title: Nila Spaces (NSE:NILASPACES) Posted Healthy Earnings But There Are Some Other Factors To Be Aware Of
data.description:
Last week's profit announcement from Nila Spaces Limited (NSE:NILASPACES) was underwhelming for investors, despite headline numbers being robust. Our analysis uncovered some concerning factors that we believe the market might be paying attention to.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

A Closer Look At Nila Spaces' Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Over the twelve months to September 2026, Nila Spaces recorded an accrual ratio of 0.88. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. To wit, the company did not generate one whit of free cashflow in that time. Even though it reported a profit of ₹315.9m, a look at free cash flow indicates it actually burnt through ₹2.8b in the last year. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of ₹2.8b, this year, indicates high risk.

Our Take On Nila Spaces' Profit Performance

As we have made quite clear, we're a bit worried that Nila Spaces didn't back up the last year's profit with free cashflow. For this reason, we think that Nila Spaces' statutory profits may be a bad guide to its underlying earnings power, and might give investors an overly positive impression of the company. But at least holders can take some solace from the 58% EPS growth in the last year. Of course, we've only just scratched the surface when it comes to analysing its earnings; one could also consider margins, forecast growth, and return on investment, among other factors.
